content: 1. The updated guidelines from May 24, 2010, include significant revisions, which are highlighted and discussed throughout the document. 2. Recommendations for the use of antiretroviral (ARV) drugs in pregnant women infected with HIV-1 are provided to improve maternal health and reduce perinatal HIV transmission in the United States. 3. A two-week public comment period follows the release of the updated guidelines on the AIDSinfo website, during which the public can submit feedback. 4. The panel reviews public comments to determine if additional revisions to the guidelines are necessary. 5. Updates include recent findings from international clinical trials, such as HPTN 046, which showed that extending infant nevirapine prophylaxis from 6 weeks to 6 months reduces postnatal infections, and NICHD-HPTN 040/PACTG 1043, which demonstrated that combination infant ARV prophylaxis is more effective than the standard 6-week zidovudine regimen in formula-fed infants when mothers have not received antepartum ARV drugs. 6. A new subsection on reproductive options for HIV-concordant and serodiscordant couples is included, discussing the HPTN 052 trial, which showed that initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) in individuals with CD4 counts between 350 and 550 cells/mm³ reduces transmission risk to seronegative partners. 7. Table 4 has been added to address drug interactions between hormonal contraceptives and ARV agents. 8. Table 5 has been revised to include drug formulation, dosing information, pregnancy-related pharmacokinetics, toxicity data, and recommendations for ARV use during pregnancy. The newly approved drug rilpivirine is also included. 9. Expanded discussions on treatment recommendations for adults and postpartum discontinuation of ARV regimens are provided. 10. Tenofovir has been reclassified as a preferred nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) for women co-infected with HIV and hepatitis B virus (HBV). 11. Indinavir and nelfinavir have been moved to the category of protease inhibitors (PIs) for use in special circumstances. 12. For ARV-naive pregnant women, early and sustained control of HIV viral replication is emphasized, with data supporting the initiation of ARV drugs as early as possible in pregnancy to reduce transmission risk. 13. For HIV/HBV co-infected pregnant women, combination ARV regimens including anti-HBV drugs are recommended, with tenofovir plus lamivudine or emtricitabine as the preferred dual NRTI/NtRTI backbone. 14. A new section addresses the diagnosis and management of acute HIV-1 infection during pregnancy. 15. Another new section discusses the diagnosis and management of HIV-2 infection in pregnancy. 16. Data from new studies on preterm delivery and combination ARV regimens are reviewed, noting a possible small increased risk of preterm birth with PI-based regimens but emphasizing their benefits for maternal health and prevention of mother-to-child transmission. 17. Based on NICHD-HPTN 040/PACTG 1043 trial results, intrapartum single-dose nevirapine is no longer recommended for HIV-infected women in labor who have not received antepartum drugs. Instead, intravenous zidovudine and infant combination ARV prophylaxis for 6 weeks are recommended. 18. Postpartum care includes expanded discussions on stopping ARVs, counseling on safer sex practices, and contraception during the postpartum period. 19. Twice-daily dosing is now recommended for the 6-week zidovudine prophylaxis regimen in full-term infants, with a dose of 4 mg/kg body weight orally twice daily starting as soon as possible after birth, preferably within 6-12 hours of delivery. 20. The design and results of the NICHD-HPTN 040/PACTG 1043 trial in formula-fed infants are discussed, showing that a 2-drug regimen of zidovudine and nevirapine is as effective as a 3-drug regimen but with lower toxicity. 21. A new subsection addresses the management of breastfeeding infants of mothers first diagnosed with HIV during the postpartum period. 22. The guidelines aim to provide healthcare providers with information to discuss with HIV-infected pregnant women, enabling informed decisions about ARV use during pregnancy and scheduled cesarean delivery to reduce perinatal HIV transmission. 23. The panel recognizes that strategies for preventing perinatal transmission and managing HIV in pregnant women are rapidly evolving and will adjust recommendations as new evidence emerges. 24. The guidelines are structured to reflect the management of individual mother-child pairs, covering preconception care, and principles for managing the woman and her infant during the antepartum, intrapartum, and postpartum periods. 25. While perinatal HIV transmission occurs worldwide, these recommendations are specifically developed for use in the United States, with alternative strategies potentially appropriate in other countries based on local considerations. 26. The panel meets monthly to review data that may warrant guideline modifications, with updates prompted by new drug approvals, safety or efficacy data, or other clinically significant information. 27. Recommendations are based on scientific evidence and expert opinion, with each statement rated for strength and quality of evidence. 28. 29. Combined antepartum, intrapartum, and infant ARV prophylaxis is recommended to prevent perinatal HIV transmission. 30. Breastfeeding is not recommended for HIV-infected women in the United States due to the availability of safe, affordable, and feasible alternatives.
